lessons.title: Oral English: discussion, debate and listening
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)

objectives: Take part in a discussion politely.
Present an argument in a short debate speech.
Listen for the main points and take notes.

blocks.md: Speaking and listening are tested in class and in oral examinations. In **discussions** and **debates** you give your opinion, listen to others and respond politely. Good speakers are clear, organised and respectful.

blocks.title: Useful expressions
blocks.md:
- **Agreeing:** *I agree with you; That is a good point.*
- **Disagreeing politely:** *I see your point, but...; I am afraid I disagree because...*
- **Giving an opinion:** *In my view...; I believe that...*
- **Asking for clarification:** *Could you explain what you mean?*
- **Interrupting politely:** *Excuse me, may I add something?*
Avoid shouting, insults and personal attacks.

blocks.caption: Polite phrases keep a debate friendly.
blocks.alt: A table of debate language: agree, that is a good point; disagree, I see it differently; clarify, what do you mean; conclude, to sum up.

blocks.title: Speaking and listening skills
blocks.md:
- **Speaking:** make one clear point at a time, support it with a reason, look at your audience, speak slowly and loudly enough.
- **Debate speech:** greet the chair and audience (*Mr Chairman, honourable members*), state your side, give two reasons, answer the other side, thank them.
- **Listening:** listen for **key words**, write short **notes**, and wait before replying.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Interrupting rudely or speaking too long.
- Attacking the person instead of the idea.
- Reading a text word for word without looking at the audience.
- Speaking too fast or too softly.
- Not listening and repeating what has been said.

blocks.title: Example 1: disagree politely
blocks.statement: Someone says *School should start at eight, not seven.* You disagree. What can you say?
steps: Acknowledge their view first, then give your reason.
*I see your point, but a seven o'clock start gives us a longer afternoon for sports.*
blocks.answer: I see your point, but a seven o'clock start gives us a longer afternoon for sports.

blocks.title: Example 2: a debate opening
blocks.statement: Write the opening sentences of a speech supporting the motion *Pupils should learn a trade in secondary school.*
steps: Address the chair and audience, then state your side.
Mr Chairman, honourable members, I stand firmly in support of the motion.
blocks.answer: Mr Chairman, honourable members, ladies and gentlemen, I stand firmly in support of the motion that pupils should learn a trade in secondary school.

exercises.prompt: Write a one-minute speech (about 120 words) for the motion *Mobile phones should be banned from secondary schools*. Choose your side. Include a greeting, two reasons, a reply to the other side and thanks.
exercises.model: Mr Chairman, honourable members, I stand in support of the motion. Firstly, phones distract pupils during lessons. Secondly, they can be used for cheating. Some say phones help research, but the school library and computer room are better places. For these reasons I urge you to support the motion. Thank you.
rubric: 1 mark: answer to the opposing view.
